description: Tenochtitlán, the tribute system, codices and the ritual of human sacrifice that shocked the Spanish.
content_html:
The Aztec Empire and the Triple Alliance

By the early sixteenth century, the Aztec Triple Alliance dominated central Mexico. Formed in 1428, the alliance united three city-states: Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan. Historians often use the terms “Aztec Empire” and “Mexica” interchangeably; the people of Tenochtitlan called themselves the Mexica. At its peak, the empire controlled a vast territory with a population estimated at between five and six million people across roughly 500 subject towns.

The empire was not a unified state in the modern sense. The Aztecs preferred to extract tribute from conquered peoples rather than directly administer them. Subject rulers kept local control as long as they paid tribute on time and provided warriors for Aztec campaigns. Those who refused or rebelled were crushed with overwhelming force, and their population could be taken for sacrifice. This system created prosperity at the centre but resentment among tributary peoples — resentment that Cortés would later exploit.

Tenochtitlán: The Island City

Tenochtitlán was built on an island in Lake Texcoco, connected to the mainland by three great causeways. The city’s grid of streets, canals and aqueducts astonished the Spanish when they arrived. Contemporary estimates put its population at between 200,000 and 300,000 — larger than London or Paris at the time. At its heart stood the Templo Mayor (“Great Temple”), a massive pyramid-shaped structure dedicated to the two principal Aztec deities, Huitzilopochtli (god of the sun and war) and Tlaloc (god of rain and agriculture).

Key Fact

Tenochtitlán was built on an island in Lake Texcoco and had a population of approximately 200,000–300,000 by 1500 — larger than any city in Europe at the time. The Templo Mayor at its centre was dedicated to the sun god Huitzilopochtli and the rain god Tlaloc.

Methods of Rule and the Tribute System

The tribute system was the economic foundation of Aztec power. Twice a year, subject towns sent goods to Tenochtitlán: maize, beans, cacao, cotton cloth, rubber, feathers, jade, gold dust and live animals. The famous Aztec “tribute rolls” — pictorial records of who paid what — list goods from hundreds of towns. The tribute sustained the elite, fed the capital’s population and funded warfare. Merchants (known as pochteca) operated long-distance trade networks across Mexico, bringing luxury goods to the capital.

Aztec society was hierarchical. At the top was the huey tlatoani (“great speaker”), the emperor. Below him were nobles, priests, warriors and merchants. Commoners farmed tribute lands or practised crafts. At the bottom were slaves, who could be sold but could also buy their freedom. Social mobility was possible through military success: a commoner who captured several enemy warriors could rise to the warrior nobility.

Codices were Aztec pictorial books made from bark paper or deerskin, folded like a screen. They recorded history, religious calendars, astronomical observations, tribute lists and ritual knowledge. Trained scribes (tlacuilos) produced them. Most of the pre-conquest codices were destroyed by Spanish missionaries who saw them as works of the devil; only a handful of pre-conquest Aztec codices survive. Post-conquest codices — many produced by indigenous scribes working alongside Spanish friars — are the main written record of Aztec civilisation. The most important post-conquest compilation is the Florentine Codex, compiled by Friar Bernardino de Sahagún in the 1570s using Nahua informants, which records Aztec history, culture and religion in extraordinary detail.

Aztec Religion and Human Sacrifice

Aztec religion was polytheistic — the Aztecs worshipped many gods. The most important was Huitzilopochtli, the sun and war god. The Aztecs believed that the sun — and by extension, all life — required constant nourishment with human blood. Without it, the sun would cease to move and the world would end. This cosmological belief was the religious justification for human sacrifice on a large scale.

Sacrifices typically took place at the top of the Templo Mayor. A priest cut open the victim’s chest and removed the still-beating heart, offering it to Huitzilopochtli. The body was then rolled down the temple steps. Most victims were war captives — which is why the Aztecs valued live capture over killing in battle, and why they engaged in the “Flower Wars” (ritual battles with neighbouring states specifically to take prisoners for sacrifice). The scale of sacrifice is debated: Spanish chroniclers gave wildly inflated figures; modern estimates range from hundreds to tens of thousands per year, concentrated at major religious festivals.

Key Fact

The Aztecs practised human sacrifice because they believed the sun god Huitzilopochtli required human blood to continue moving across the sky. Most sacrifices took place at the Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlán, using war captives taken in the “Flower Wars.”

Quetzalcoatl was one of the most important deities in Mesoamerican religion — the feathered serpent, associated with wind, learning and the planet Venus. Some later colonial-era sources claimed that Moctezuma II believed Cortés was the returning Quetzalcoatl, explaining why the Aztecs initially received him without attacking. Most modern historians are sceptical of this account: the identification of Cortés with Quetzalcoatl appears mainly in post-conquest sources produced decades after the events and may reflect the interests of indigenous groups who collaborated with the Spanish rather than Aztec belief at the time of contact.
exam_tip_html: When answering a “Describe two features” question about the Aztec civilisation, make sure you include a development for full marks — do not just name a feature. For example, “The Aztecs had a tribute system” is one mark; “The Aztecs extracted tribute twice yearly from subject towns, including food, textiles, gold and warriors, which sustained the capital and funded warfare” is two marks. For the 12-mark interpretation question, remember to both agree and disagree with the interpretation before reaching a substantiated conclusion. Do not write one-sided responses.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Aztec Triple Alliance, formed in 1428, ruled central Mexico through a tribute system extracting goods from hundreds of subject towns; Tenochtitlán, the capital built on Lake Texcoco, had a population of 200,000–300,000 — larger than any city in contemporary Europe.
  • Aztec religion was polytheistic; the sun god Huitzilopochtli was believed to require regular human blood sacrifice to keep the sun moving. Sacrifices mainly used war captives taken in the “Flower Wars,” and took place at the Templo Mayor.
  • Aztec codices — pictorial manuscripts recording history, religion and tribute — were mostly destroyed by Spanish missionaries; the post-conquest Florentine Codex, compiled by Friar Sahagún in the 1570s, is now the main written source for Aztec civilisation.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Aztec tribute system.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying a feature (e.g. subject towns paid goods twice yearly / goods included maize, textiles, gold, cacao / failure to pay resulted in military punishment). Two marks for a developed explanation of its significance for Aztec power.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Tenochtitlán that made it an impressive city by early sixteenth-century standards.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It was built on an island in Lake Texcoco, connected by three great causeways, with canals and an aqueduct supply system.
• It had a population of 200,000–300,000 — larger than any contemporary European city.
• At its centre stood the Templo Mayor, a massive pyramid dedicated to Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc.
• The market at Tlatelolco was described by Spanish observers as larger and better organised than any in Europe.
[2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of human sacrifice in Aztec religion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies the cosmological belief that Huitzilopochtli required human blood to sustain the movement of the sun, and develops this fully — the Aztecs believed the sun would stop if sacrifice ceased, meaning all life would end; the “Flower Wars” with neighbouring states were specifically organised to supply captives for this purpose; links to the Templo Mayor as the central site.
Secure: Identifies a cause with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Names a cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague statement without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Aztec tribute system for the peoples of central Mexico.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that the tribute system created deep resentment among subject peoples who paid goods and supplied sacrificial victims; this resentment meant that groups like the Tlaxcalans were willing to ally with Cortés against the Aztecs in 1519 — a consequence that directly contributed to the empire’s fall. Links specific evidence.
Secure: Identifies consequence with supporting evidence.
Developing: States a consequence with basic explanation.
Emerging: Brief point without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Aztec codices as a historical source.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses significance at the time (codices recorded history, religion, tribute and astronomical knowledge; scribes maintained cultural memory; destroyed by Spanish, so pre-conquest ones are rare) AND over time (post-conquest codices like the Florentine Codex are the main written record of Aztec civilisation; used by historians to understand Aztec society from an indigenous perspective). Developed with evidence.
Secure: Addresses significance with evidence; may lack the over-time dimension fully.
Developing: Describes what codices are without fully analysing significance.
Emerging: Brief or general points only.

practice_questions.text: 'Human sacrifice was the most important feature of Aztec civilisation.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the interpretation:
• Human sacrifice was central to Aztec cosmology — without it, the Aztecs believed the sun would stop; it shaped political and military strategy (Flower Wars, tribute of captives).
• It was the feature that most shocked Spanish observers and shaped European representations of the Aztecs.
• The Templo Mayor — the physical and spiritual heart of the empire — was primarily a sacrificial site.

Arguments challenging the interpretation:
• The tribute system was arguably more important as the economic foundation of Aztec power; it sustained the capital, funded warfare and bound hundreds of towns into the empire.
• Tenochtitlán’s urban sophistication (grid plan, aqueducts, large population) reflects advanced civilisation beyond religion.
• The codices show a complex intellectual and administrative culture that goes far beyond sacrifice.

Mastering: Sustained argument, agrees AND disagrees with evidence, substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some relevant points, limited judgement.
Emerging: Descriptive, no evaluation.

options: An agreement between the Aztecs, the Spanish and the Tlaxcalans
A religious union between the three Aztec gods
A political union of three city-states — Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan — formed in 1428
A trade agreement between three central Mexican kingdoms

glossary_terms.definition: A political union of three city-states — Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan — formed in 1428 that dominated central Mexico until the Spanish conquest.
The capital city of the Aztec Empire, built on an island in Lake Texcoco with a population of approximately 200,000–300,000 by 1500.
The Aztec system requiring conquered peoples to deliver regular payments of goods — food, textiles, gold, cacao — to the rulers in Tenochtitlán.
Aztec pictorial manuscripts recording history, religion, tribute records and astronomical observations; most pre-conquest examples were destroyed by Spanish missionaries.
The Aztec god of the sun and war, principal deity of Tenochtitlán, believed to require human blood to sustain the movement of the sun.
The feathered serpent deity of Mesoamerican religion, associated with wind, learning and Venus; in some traditions prophesied to return from the east.
